I've been wanting to move to the pacific northwest for a while, but I don't have any relatives in the area and the thought of being so far from anyone I know if things were to go wrong is kind of daunting. How much should I save up beforehand? Is it hard to get a job ahead of time? Tips in general on trying to get started somewhere new?

Are you looking to live in a city, the suburbs, somewhere rural? Makes a pretty big difference planning wise.

IIf moving alone, that's just life - you can't be looking for a potential crutch, just plan well. Have a plan for if your money runs out, a plan for if you can't find a job. I'd save enough money for gas/bus/plane just in case the whole move doesn't work.

Save a lot of money. Just moving into a new place usually means two months rent up front, Utilities activation fees and deposits. If you use your own truck (which is a bad idea since you won't have anyone to help) they guzzle gas and after a couple hundred miles will start charging by the mile. Actual movers or shipping your stuff will be very expensive as well. Moving 3 hours from my last place was around $3000 of extra expenses (including the deposit on the new place).

The first month will hurt.

Job markets differ everywhere, but it doesn't hurt to start applying.

If you jump in blind, you're asking for trouble, but sometimes you don't have a choice. Job markets vary widely no matter where you go. I'd personally save for 2 months of normal expenses (plus the cost of a deposit for an apartment in your new area), quite a bit more if you have others to support on your dime.

Outside of that, just meet new people and start networking as soon as you can. When you're on a timer with your living expenses, finding a job has to be priority #1. It also worth noting, I've had dozens of jobs in my life, but never once have I gone in for a suit-and-tie interview. Networking and making a good impression is more than enough to get you a job, but you have to be clean-cut and able to work harder than the other guy. So there is a trade off.

Good luck with your adventure, and maybe plan ahead to have a job to move home to, if your initial move doesn't work out for you.

I've done this a few times (for school, for jobs, etc.). I assume you are an individual guy and not moving a family so you can take more risks. As others have pointed out, it is best to sell most of your stuff (or leave it with others) because the more you have, the harder it will be. Also do what you can to cut your monthly expenses (consider cheaper cell phone services, no cable, etc.). The more you save up the more likely you are to succeed (6 months of expenses is ideal, 3 months is pretty good, less than that and it will be tough).

First thing, figure out your plan B - if things don't work out, what will you do? Usually, this means saving up enough to buy a ticket back "home" wherever that is.

Find a place to live for cheap (usually someone looking for a roommate on Craigslist) without a commitment - this helps your money last longer and you can always move later. Don't be picky on people, you just need a cheap place that is safe (having fewer possessions helps because you don't have to worry about your roommate breaking/stealing/ruining your stuff). The lower your expenses, the longer your savings last. It is best to find a job before you go, but this can be very hard depending on your occupation. Make sure you have what you need to be employed (e.g., if you are a nurse, get certified in the new state).

Once you have a place lined up and money saved, you can move to the new state. Next, focus on a job. If you have a car, you may consider temporary "jobs" like Uber or Lyft but that is likely not your long term solution. Getting a job can be tough, so look for cheap entertainment and stick to a routine to keep you motivated. For example, wake up each day, apply for a couple jobs, then go to the library to read and entertain yourself for a while. Cook your meals to save money (ramen is cheap, but you don't necessarily have to go to that extreme).

Once you have a job and are no longer worried about having to leave the state, you can spend a lot more time making friends and enjoying your new home. You can consider moving to a place of your own or a nicer place, or whatever you want. Congrats on the move.

Getting a job in the NW is like anywhere else. You definitely want to visit and interview before moving because the savings go fast. How much you need depends on if you bring a car, work clothes, towels, something to sleep on, something to cook with, and if you can stay at someone's place for a month or two. Otherwise you're looking at $200 per day for a hotel (140), car rental (40), and groceries (20). A lot of urban areas have better public transit than other states though, so it's possible to go without a car.

Getting an apartment will probably require first + last + deposit, and you might not get paid until almost 30 days from your hire date.

Most importantly, get plenty of rest!

I moved in 2008 to San Francisco without knowing a single soul or ever being to California. I had the promise of a job that paid practically minimum wage and $3,000. It was three years before I could ever afford to fly home (lived in the mid-west). I've been living in CA for seven years now and haven't regretted it once.

I came with only two suitcases of clothes. When I moved last year from SF to San Diego I had a uhaul full of furniture, a car, a newly earned Masters degree, great friends/memories, and a new husband. Today I have a new daughter. BEST DECISION I EVER MADE IN MY LIFE!

However sacrifices will have to be made depending on your income and job market worth. I spent the first three years without a car huffing it on foot or public transit. I lived in ghetto studio apartments or in uncomfortable Craigslist roommate situations, and I went through three major jobs.

With all that being said - I also know people who have come out here and failed spectacularly. I think you have to be determined that "going back" is not an option, have marketable skills to get work when needed, unbelievable low standards to "be ok" with your crap living situation, a little bit of luck (or Devine blessing), and a sense of adventure.
